claim: The glomerular basement membrane (GBM) is an essential mediator of glomerular ultrafiltration.
source: the kidney glomerular basement membrane (GBM), an essential mediator of glomerular ultrafiltration
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about GBM function

claim: STORM and STORM-electron microscopy correlation revealed a laminar organization of ECM proteins within the GBM.
source: Using multichannel STORM and STORM-electron microscopy correlation, we constructed a molecular reference frame that revealed a laminar organization of ECM proteins within the GBM.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the study

claim: Analyses of domains near the N- and C-termini of agrin, laminin, and collagen IV in mouse and human GBM revealed a highly oriented macromolecular organization.
source: Separate analyses of domains near the N- and C-termini of agrin, laminin, and collagen IV in mouse and human GBM revealed a highly oriented macromolecular organization.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the study

claim: Disruptions in GBM architecture were observed in a mouse model of Alport syndrome.
source: Our analysis also revealed disruptions in this GBM architecture in a mouse model of Alport syndrome.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the study

claim: The glomerular filtration barrier (GFB) is organized into three major layers: endothelial cells with fenestrations, podocytes with foot processes, and the glomerular basement membrane.
source: The GFB is organized into three major layers: (1) endothelial cells with fenestrations that line the glomerular capillaries; (2) unique epithelial cells called podocytes that extend many 'foot' processes that interdigitate with those of adjacent podocytes and are linked to each other via a specialized cell/cell junction called the slit diaphragm; and (3) the glomerular basement membrane (GBM)
evidence: This is established knowledge about GFB structure, supported by citation to Miner, 2011

claim: The GBM is composed of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins secreted by endothelial cells and podocytes.
source: the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), which is composed of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins secreted by the endothelial cells and podocytes that flank it
evidence: This is established knowledge about GBM composition, supported by citation to Miner, 2011

claim: The GFB allows unimpeded passage of water and small solutes while restricting passage of plasma proteins such as albumin and immunoglobulins.
source: The GFB's major physiological role is to allow the unimpeded passage of water and small solutes (including metabolic waste products) from the bloodstream into the urinary space, while restricting the passage of plasma proteins such as albumin and immunoglobulins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GFB function

claim: Injuries or genetic defects in any one of the three GFB layers can cause GFB malfunction resulting in increased protein in the urine.
source: it is clear that injuries or genetic defects in any one of the three layers can cause GFB malfunction that results in increased levels of protein in the urine, a hallmark of diverse kidney diseases
evidence: This is established knowledge about GFB pathology

claim: The GBM contains specific isoforms of laminin (laminin α5β2γ1, or LM-521), type IV collagen (primarily the collagen α3α4α5(IV) network), heparan sulfate proteoglycan (primarily agrin), and nidogen.
source: The GBM contains specific isoforms of laminin (laminin α5β2γ1, or LM-521), type IV collagen (primarily the collagen α3α4α5(IV) network), heparan sulfate proteoglycan (HSPG) (primarily agrin), and nidogen
evidence: This is established knowledge about GBM composition, supported by citation to Miner, 2012

claim: Laminin and type IV collagen self-polymerize into networks that are connected to each other and/or to cell surface receptors by HSPGs and nidogen.
source: Laminin and type IV collagen self-polymerize into networks that are connected to each other and/or to cell surface receptors by HSPGs and nidogen
evidence: This is established knowledge about ECM protein interactions, supported by citation to Yurchenco et al., 2004

claim: A systematic analysis of the actual spatial arrangement of ECM components within basement membranes has not yet been performed in vivo.
source: However, a systematic analysis of the actual spatial arrangement of ECM components within basement membranes, with respect to each other and to their receptors, has not yet been performed in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses

claim: The GFB with the GBM cannot yet be reconstituted in vitro.
source: First, the GFB with the GBM cannot yet be reconstituted in vitro.
evidence: This is a statement about current technical limitations

claim: The ∼200-nm thickness of a typical mouse GBM is close to the diffraction limited resolution of conventional light microscopy.
source: Second, the ∼200-nm thickness of a typical mouse GBM is close to the diffraction limited resolution of conventional light microscopy, thus preventing its use to analyze GBM ultrastructural and macromolecular organization.
evidence: This is a statement about technical limitations based on known properties of light microscopy and GBM dimensions

claim: Transmission electron microscopy studies show electron dense and translucent layers (lamina densa and lamina lucida) in the GBM.

evidence: This is established knowledge from EM studies, supported by citation to Chan et al., 1993

claim: It is unclear whether the electron dense and translucent layers observed by EM reflect an organization of proteins in the GBM.
source: Transmission electron microscopy (EM) studies show electron dense and translucent layers (lamina densa and lamina lucida), but it is unclear whether these reflect an organization of proteins in the GBM
evidence: This is a statement about uncertainty in the interpretation of EM data

claim: Super-resolution light microscopic approaches have broken the diffraction limit of light microscopy, combining nanoscopic image resolution with high efficiency and multi-color labeling.

evidence: This is established knowledge about super-resolution microscopy, supported by citations to Huang et al., 2009; Ji et al., 2008; Hell, 2009

claim: Single molecule localization-based imaging methods such as (F)PALM and STORM achieve molecular scale resolution.
source: In particular, single molecule localization-based imaging methods such as (fluorescence) photoactivable localization microscopy ((F)PALM) and stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (STORM) (Betzig et al., 2006; Hess et al., 2006; Rust et al., 2006) achieve a molecular scale resolution

claim: Sub-diffraction microscopy methods have been used to dissect the nanoscale architecture of multi-protein complexes in neuronal synapses, adhesion complexes, centrosomes, and the nuclear pore complex.
